languages.you: Use మీరు (polite) when speaking to a developer or customer; నువ్వు is for close friends and children.
languages.register: Write the modern spoken-standard style (వ్యవహారిక భాష), not literary (గ్రాంథిక) Telugu. Prefer a common Telugu word over a Sanskrit one when both exist.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in technical and business text. Telugu numerals (౦-౯) look dated in apps and forms.
script_notes: Words are long because Telugu attaches endings to them (agglutination), so a 15-word limit is tight; split sentences early.
A zero-width non-joiner (U+200C) is used before some endings, as in స్టేషన్‌లో. Keep it when present, never add stray ones.
languages.loanwords: Everyday English loanwords written in Telugu script (బస్, ఫోన్, బ్యాంక్) are fine. For abstract ideas prefer the Telugu word.

languages.you: आप is the safe default. तुम is for friends and juniors, तू only for very close people or children.
languages.register: Use spoken Hindustani that people actually say. Avoid heavy Sanskritised words (शुद्ध हिन्दी) in conversation, and avoid Urdu-heavy words in formal notices where a plain alternative exists.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in apps and forms. Devanagari numerals (०-९) appear in print and government text.
script_notes: End sentences with the danda (।). Question marks are written as ?.
The nukta letters (क़ ख़ ग़ ज़ ड़ ढ़ फ़) keep Urdu and English sounds; many typists drop the dot, and both spellings should be accepted.
languages.loanwords: English words common in Hindi speech (मोबाइल, बैंक, फ़ोन) are natural. Do not force a Sanskrit coinage for them.

languages.you: Use நீங்கள் (polite) by default. நீ is for close friends and younger people.
languages.register: Tamil has a wide gap between written and spoken forms. Write the standard written form in notices and reports, and keep the colloquial form for casual chat and speech output.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in apps. Tamil numerals (௦-௯) are rare today.
script_notes: Grantha letters (ஜ ஷ ஸ ஹ க்ஷ) are used for loanwords and names. Do not replace them with native letters in names.
languages.loanwords: Prefer a Tamil word where one is in real use; Tamil readers notice and appreciate it. Keep brand names and technical acronyms as they are.

languages.you: ನೀವು is the polite form; ನೀನು is informal.
languages.register: Written Kannada (ಗ್ರಂಥಿಕ) and spoken Kannada (ಆಡುಮಾತು) differ. Use the plain, widely understood standard for notices.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in apps. Kannada numerals (೦-೯) are used in print.
script_notes: Agglutinative like Telugu, so words are long and sentences carry fewer words.
languages.loanwords: English loanwords in Kannada script are common (ಬ್ಯಾಂಕ್, ಮೊಬೈಲ್). Prefer Kannada for abstract ideas.

languages.you: നിങ്ങൾ is polite; നീ is informal.
languages.register: Malayalam builds very long compound words, so sentences hold fewer words. Keep sentences short and avoid stacking clauses.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in apps. Malayalam numerals are rare.
script_notes: Use the atomic chillu letters (ൻ ൽ ർ ൾ ൺ). The older ZWJ-based spellings render differently in different fonts.
Check that text is normalised to NFC; Malayalam is where mixed encodings cause the most visible breakage.
languages.loanwords: English loanwords are written in Malayalam script (ബാങ്ക്, ഫോൺ).

languages.you: तुम्ही is polite and the right default; तू is informal.
languages.register: Use everyday Marathi. Marathi shares a script with Hindi, so check the words too: Hindi words in Marathi text read as wrong.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in apps. Devanagari numerals (०-९) are common in print.
script_notes: Marathi uses the letter ळ, which Hindi does not. Modern Marathi ends sentences with a full stop (.), not the danda.
languages.loanwords: English loanwords in Devanagari are common (बँक, मोबाईल).

languages.you: আপনি is polite, তুমি is familiar, তুই is intimate. Verb endings change with each.
languages.register: Standard colloquial Bengali (চলিত ভাষা) is right for almost everything. The formal literary style (সাধু ভাষা) is out of use.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in apps. Bengali numerals (০-৯) are common in print.
languages.loanwords: English loanwords in Bengali script are common (ব্যাংক, মোবাইল).

languages.you: તમે is polite; આપ is very formal; તું is informal.
languages.register: Use plain, modern Gujarati. Gujarati does not use the danda; sentences end with a full stop.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in apps. Gujarati numerals (૦-૯) are used in print.
script_notes: There is no horizontal headline bar, so letters are easy to confuse at small sizes. Prefer a font size of 16px or more.
languages.loanwords: English loanwords in Gujarati script are common.

languages.you: ਤੁਸੀਂ is polite; ਤੂੰ is informal.
languages.register: Punjabi is written in Gurmukhi in India. Shahmukhi (Perso-Arabic) is a different script used in Pakistan; do not mix them.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in apps. Gurmukhi numerals (੦-੯) are used in print.
script_notes: End sentences with the danda (।). Tone is partly marked by letters (ਘ ਝ ਢ ਧ ਭ), so a spelling slip can change a word.
languages.loanwords: English loanwords in Gurmukhi are common.

languages.you: ଆପଣ is polite; ତୁମେ is familiar.
languages.register: Use plain standard Odia. Note: the realtime speech endpoint calls Odia or-IN, while every other Sarvam endpoint calls it od-IN.
languages.digits: Use 0-9 in apps. Odia numerals (୦-୯) are used in print.
script_notes: End sentences with the danda (।). Check the letters ଡ଼ and ଢ଼ (with a dot below); they are often typed wrongly.
languages.loanwords: English loanwords in Odia script are common.

languages.you: Plain 'you'. Avoid slang, and idioms that do not translate.
languages.register: Indian English: mostly British spelling (colour, centre), lakh and crore for large amounts, dates as DD/MM/YYYY, the ₹ sign before the amount.
languages.digits: Use 0-9. Group digits the Indian way (12,50,000) when writing rupee amounts for Indian readers.
